question: Most electric vehicles use lithium-ion batteries, for which the value chain is 95% controlled by China, Japan and South Korea. China currently has predominant control over the value chain for the vast majority of the chemical and metallurgical products needed to make lithium-ion batteries.

The primary interest in recycling batteries would therefore be to make savings in materials, allowing the EU to reduce its dependence on Asian inputs. In addition, recycling electric batteries could reduce the carbon footprint by 28%. Globally, the battery recycling industry is still in its infancy, which makes it a great opportunity for Europe. 1.
How will the Commission contribute to the integration of recycling facilities at European level?

Does the Commission intend to invest in recycling projects so that the European Union can have industrial control over new, more efficient and less polluting processes and gain a real competitive advantage?
If so, will the Commission free up resources within existing research and development programmes (Horizon, Important Projects of Common European Interest)?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.1.2025) 1. The Batteries Regulation1 and secondary legislation will ensure that the conditions for all recycling facilities will be the same, enabling a smooth cooperation along the EU recycling value chain. 2.

Under Horizon Europe2, the Commission has established the co-programmed partnership on battery research and innovation BATT4EU providing an EU investment of up to EUR 925 million. This partnership covers the full value chain and so far EUR 115 million (i.e. ~19% of the presently allocated budget) are going into recycling and circularity.
Beyond Horizon Europe, the Innovation Fund3 funds innovative projects that reduce greenhouse gas emissions, with battery recycling in scope and 4 projects already funded.

Under State aid rules, the Commission has approved two battery related Important Projects of Common European Interest (IPCEIs)4 that cover recycling and refining, providing EUR 6 billion in public funding, by the participating Member States, unlocking EUR ~14 billion in private investments.

The Joint European Forum for IPCEI (JEF-IPCEI), a partnership between the Commission and the Member States, has endorsed a proposed IPCEI candidate on circular advanced materials for clean technologies on 27 November 2024. Member States will work on the design of this IPCEI candidate. 3. The next call for BATT4EU is to be published early 2025 and the Work Programme 202627 is to be developed.
Battery recycling will remain an integral part. Innovative battery recycling projects remain eligible for the Innovation Fund.
1 Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 July 2023 concerning

batteries and waste batteries, amending Directive 2008/98/EC and Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and repealing Directive 2006/66/EC, OJ L 191, 28.7.2023, p. 1–117. 2 https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-opencalls/horizon-europe_en 3 https://cinea.ec.europa.eu/programmes/innovation-fund_en 4 https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/state-aid/ipcei/approved-ipceis/batteries-value-chain_en
